size: 6–8 ft long incl. tail (1.8–2.4 m), 2–2.5 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: A mountain lion can leap about 15 feet straight up, onto a ledge or into a tree, in a single bound.

size: 2.5–3.5 ft long (75–105 cm), about 2 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Bobcats are named for their short, stubby 'bobbed' tail, only 4–7 inches long.

size: 3.5–4.5 ft long incl. tail (1.1–1.4 m), about 2 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Coyotes can sprint up to 40 mph and live in every part of California, including downtown Los Angeles.

size: 2.5–3.5 ft long incl. tail (80–110 cm), about 14 in tall at shoulder
fun_fact: The gray fox is one of the only members of the dog family that can climb trees.

size: 4–6 ft long (1.2–1.8 m), 2.5–3 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Most of California's 'black' bears are actually brown, cinnamon or blond.

size: 4–7 ft long (1.2–2.1 m), 3–3.5 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Mule deer are named for their huge, mule-like ears, which swivel separately to track sounds.

size: 6.5–8 ft long (2–2.5 m), 4–5 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: The Tule elk, found only in California, dropped to fewer than 30 animals in the 1870s and has recovered to over 5,000.

size: 4.5–6 ft long (1.4–1.8 m), about 3 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: A ram's curled horns can weigh 30 pounds, as much as all the bones in its body.
Raccoons have super-sensitive front paws and often 'see' food by feeling it, especially when it's wet.
A skunk can spray accurately up to about 10 feet, and usually stamps its feet as a warning first.
The opossum is North America's only marsupial; babies ride in a pouch, then on their mother's back.
Western gray squirrels bury thousands of acorns each fall and forget many of them, planting new oak trees.
Fox squirrels aren't native to California; they were brought in during the early 1900s and spread through cities.
These squirrels chew shed rattlesnake skins and lick the scent onto their fur to disguise their smell.
Desert cottontails rarely drink; they get most of their water from the plants they eat.
Brush rabbits rarely stray more than a few hops from dense cover and thump the ground to warn each other.

size: 1.5–2 ft long (47–63 cm), ears up to 7 in
fun_fact: A jackrabbit's giant ears work like radiators, releasing body heat to keep it cool in the desert.
Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch.
River otters can hold their breath for up to 8 minutes and close their ears and nostrils underwater.

size: 6–8 ft long males, 5–6 ft females (1.5–2.4 m)
fun_fact: Sea lions can 'walk' on land by rotating their back flippers forward, which true seals can't do.
Each harbor seal has a unique spot pattern, like a fingerprint.

size: Males up to 13 ft (4 m), females up to 10 ft (3 m)
weight: Males up to 5,000 lb (2,300 kg), females 900–1,800 lb
fun_fact: Elephant seals can dive more than a mile deep and stay underwater for up to 2 hours.
Male humpbacks sing complex songs that can last 20 minutes and be heard many miles away.
Marmots can hibernate for up to 8 months a year in the high Sierra.

size: 6–8 in long (15–20 cm), no visible tail
fun_fact: Pikas don't hibernate; all summer they cut and dry 'haypiles' of plants to eat under the winter snow.
The California Quail is the state bird; its forward-curling head plume is made of six feathers.
The fierce scream you hear for eagles in movies is almost always a red-tailed hawk.
Steller's jays often imitate the red-shouldered hawk's call so well that it fools other birds.
Cooper's hawks chase small birds through thick branches at high speed, steering with their long tails.

size: 9–12 in long (22–31 cm), about 2 ft wingspan
fun_fact: The kestrel is North America's smallest falcon and can hover in place while hunting.
Bald eagle nests can grow to 10 feet wide and weigh over a ton after years of additions.
Golden eagles can dive at more than 150 mph when chasing prey.
Ospreys plunge feet-first into water and turn the fish head-forward to carry it in flight.

size: 25–32 in long (64–81 cm), about 6 ft wingspan
fun_fact: Turkey vultures can smell carrion from more than a mile away, rare for a bird.

size: 3.5–4.5 ft long (1.1–1.4 m), up to 9.5 ft wingspan
fun_fact: With a wingspan up to 9.5 feet, the condor is North America's largest flying land bird; in 1987 only 27 were left.
Great horned owls are one of the few animals that regularly hunt skunks.
Barn owls can catch mice in total darkness using hearing alone.
During courtship dives, male Anna's hummingbirds hit about 60 mph and make a chirp with their tail feathers.
Acorn woodpeckers store acorns in 'granary trees' that can hold up to 50,000 acorns, each in its own hole.
Unlike most woodpeckers, flickers mostly feed on the ground, licking up ants with a long, sticky tongue.
Scrub-jays hide thousands of food items and remember where, and even which hiding spots others watched.
Steller's jays are excellent mimics and can imitate hawks, squirrels, cats and even dogs.
Crows can recognize individual human faces and remember people who treated them badly for years.

size: 22–27 in long (56–69 cm), about 4 ft wingspan
fun_fact: Ravens are bigger than crows, have wedge-shaped tails, and do barrel rolls and somersaults in flight.
Black phoebes build cup-shaped nests out of mud, often under bridges and eaves.
Young western bluebirds often stay to help their parents raise the next brood.
Robins find earthworms mostly by sight, tilting their heads to look closely at the ground.
A male mockingbird can learn up to 200 different songs, including car alarms.
California towhees often fight their own reflections in car mirrors and windows.
White-crowned sparrows from different areas sing in local 'dialects', like regional accents.
A male house finch's red color comes from pigments in its food; the redder he is, the better he ate.
Male red-winged blackbirds puff out their red shoulder patches to defend territory and attract mates.
The yellow-billed magpie lives nowhere in the world except California's Central Valley and coastal valleys.

size: 3.2–4.5 ft tall (1–1.4 m), about 6 ft wingspan
fun_fact: Despite standing over 4 feet tall, a great blue heron weighs only about 5 pounds thanks to hollow bones.
Great egrets were nearly wiped out for their feathers in the 1800s, which led to the founding of the Audubon Society.
Brown pelicans plunge-dive from up to 60 feet and scoop up to 3 gallons of water in their pouch.
Only female mallards make the classic loud 'quack'; males make a quieter, raspy sound.
Canada geese fly in a V so each bird gets a lift from the air swirling off the wingtips of the one ahead.
Western gulls take four years to get their adult white and dark-gray feathers.

size: 20–24 in long (50–62 cm), including a long tail
fun_fact: Roadrunners can run about 20 mph and are fast enough to catch and eat rattlesnakes.
A protein in fence lizard blood kills the Lyme disease bacteria in ticks that feed on them.
Alligator lizards can drop their tails to escape predators, and the tail keeps wriggling as a distraction.
Male side-blotched lizards come in three throat colors that compete like rock, paper, scissors.
Young western skinks have bright blue tails that attract predators away from their bodies.
When threatened, horned lizards can squirt blood from their eyes up to 3 feet.
Desert iguanas stay active in heat up to 115°F, hotter than almost any other lizard can stand.
Gopher snakes hiss loudly and shake their tails to imitate rattlesnakes, but they're harmless.
Kingsnakes are immune to rattlesnake venom and sometimes eat rattlesnakes.
The San Francisco garter snake, a red, black and turquoise form, is often called America's most beautiful snake.
A rattlesnake adds a new rattle segment each time it sheds, so counting segments doesn't tell its age.
The western pond turtle is the only native freshwater turtle in most of California.

size: Shell 9–15 in long (23–38 cm), 4–6 in tall
fun_fact: Desert tortoises can live 50–80 years and spend about 95% of their lives in underground burrows.
Treefrogs can change color between green and brown in minutes to match their surroundings.
California newts carry tetrodotoxin, the same powerful poison found in pufferfish.
One rough-skinned newt has enough toxin to be deadly to a person if eaten, so never lick a newt.
Ensatinas have no lungs and breathe entirely through their moist skin.
Bullfrogs aren't native to California and will eat almost anything that fits in their mouths, including snakes and birds.
Arboreal salamanders climb up to 60 feet into oak trees and squeak when picked up.
Monarchs from the West spend winter in clusters of thousands at groves along the California coast.
Groups of tiger swallowtails gather at puddles to sip water and minerals, which is called 'puddling'.
Anise swallowtail caterpillars push out a smelly orange 'horn' called an osmeterium to scare off predators.
Pipevine swallowtails are toxic to birds because their caterpillars eat poisonous pipevine plants.
Mourning cloaks can live 10–11 months, one of the longest lifespans of any butterfly.
Painted ladies migrate in huge swarms; in 2019 a swarm over Southern California was so big it showed up on weather radar.
A honey bee does a 'waggle dance' to tell its hive the direction and distance to flowers.
Millions of convergent lady beetles gather in mountain canyons to spend winter in huge clumps.

size: 2–2.5 in long (5–6 cm), wingspan about 3.5 in
fun_fact: Male flame skimmers are bright orange-red from head to tail, even their wing veins.

size: 2.75–3 in long (7–8 cm), wingspan about 4 in
fun_fact: Green darners are among the fastest dragonflies and migrate thousands of miles, like birds.
A mantis can turn its head about 180 degrees to look over its shoulder.

size: Female body about 0.5 in (13 mm), male much smaller
fun_fact: Black widow silk is one of the strongest spider silks, and was once used for crosshairs in gun sights.
Banana slugs are the second-largest land slug in the world and the mascot of UC Santa Cruz.
When picked up, ten-lined June beetles hiss by rubbing their wings against their body.
Ochre sea stars eat mussels by pushing their stomach out of their mouth and into the shell.
Bat stars come in almost every color, from orange and red to purple, green and brown.
Purple urchins can chew holes into solid rock with their five teeth to make a home.

size: Up to 7 in tall and 10 in across (18 x 25 cm)
fun_fact: Its green color comes from tiny algae living inside its tissues, which make food from sunlight.
Lined shore crabs can hold water in their gill chambers and spend hours out of the ocean.

size: Bell up to 16 in across (40 cm), tentacles up to 15 ft
fun_fact: Sea nettles have no brain, heart or bones, and are about 95% water.
The garibaldi is California's official state marine fish, and males make clicking sounds to guard their nests.

size: 4–5 ft long (1.2–1.5 m), up to 7 ft
fun_fact: Leopard sharks gather by the hundreds in shallow, warm water off La Jolla each summer and are harmless to people.
